title: Follow the tokens
brief: Finance says the model bill doubled while traffic grew 20 percent. Before you cut anything, find where the tokens go and which lever fits. Prices, model mix, prompt shapes and the amount of agent looping are all unknown.

blocks.title: Cost per successful task
blocks.expr: cost_per_task = calls_per_task x (uncached_in x p_in + cached_in x p_cached + written_in x p_write + out x p_out) / success_rate

vars.v: model calls per task, which agent loops multiply
cached read and cache write rates, for example 0.1x and 1.25x of p_in on GPT-5.6 and later
output tokens including hidden reasoning tokens
share of tasks that finish correctly. A cheaper model with a lower rate costs more per success

blocks.example: A chat that re-sends full history across 20 turns of 500 tokens each sends 500 x (1 + 2 + ... + 20) = **105,000 input tokens** for 10,000 new ones. With an append-only prefix cached at 0.1x read and 1.25x write on the new tokens, the bill is about 95,000 x 0.1 + 10,000 x 1.25 = **22,000 token-equivalents**, roughly 79% less [[r25]]. Compaction or truncation rewrites the prefix and resets that saving.

blocks.title: Four ways to pay less per request
blocks.intro: Dials: spread of query difficulty, quality of your eval set, how the cache interacts, latency of escalation and residency of the routed models.

options.name: Static rules by task
options.summary: Send classification to a small model and reasoning-heavy work to a large one, by task type you define.
cons: Misses difficulty variation inside a task type
options.bestWhen: Clear task types and a small team.
options.avoidWhen: Difficulty varies widely inside one task type.

options.name: Trained router
options.summary: One deployment that picks a model per request. Azure's `Balanced` mode (default) targets the cheapest model within about 1% to 2% of the best quality, `Cost` within about 5% to 6%, and `Quality` favors accuracy [[r14]].
pros: RouteLLM-style routers cut cost by more than 2x in some cases with no quality loss [[r21]]
cons: Splits the prompt-cache prefix across models, so caching helps only when consecutive requests reach the same model
Context window equals the smallest underlying model, and routing reads text only
Current version 2025-11-18 updates in place, so the routed pool can change under you
options.bestWhen: Mixed difficulty and an eval set you can compare against a fixed baseline.
options.avoidWhen: Uniformly hard tasks, or a strict residency or model pin.

options.name: Cascade
options.summary: Try a cheap model, check the answer, and escalate to a stronger model only when the check fails.
pros: FrugalGPT matched the best single LLM with up to 98% lower cost, or beat GPT-4 by 4% at equal cost (2023 prices) [[r20]]
cons: Escalation adds latency and doubles spend on hard queries
Only as good as the verifier
options.bestWhen: The cheap model is right most of the time and a reliable check exists.
options.avoidWhen: Most queries are hard, or no trustworthy verifier exists.

options.name: Prompt compression
options.summary: Shrink long inputs before the call. LLMLingua reports up to 20x compression with little loss on GSM8K, BBH, ShareGPT and Arxiv-March23 [[r22]].
pros: Cuts input tokens on very long, unique contexts
cons: The compression step itself costs compute
options.bestWhen: Very long unique inputs and cost-bound batch work.
options.avoidWhen: A stable prefix that caching already handles, or text that must be quoted exactly.

stable.why: Reads at 0.1x beat uncached after two requests.

unique.why: Writes at 1.25x are never read back.

mixed.why: Works the same whatever the difficulty.

uniform.why: Works the same whatever the difficulty.

live.why: It also lowers time to first token.

stable.why: Splits the cached prefix across models.

mixed.why: Easy requests go to cheap models, so most spend drops.

uniform.why: Nothing to route, and you pay router overhead.

live.why: Escalation adds latency on hard queries.

stable.why: Discounts can stack with cached-token pricing, for example on Anthropic.

unique.why: The 50% discount does not depend on prompt shape.

live.why: A 24-hour target and no real-time SLA.

async.why: About 50% off for work nobody waits for.

stable.why: Output limits do not touch the input side.

unique.why: Output limits do not touch the input side.

mixed.why: Easy requests rarely need long answers.

uniform.why: Hidden reasoning tokens can dominate hard tasks.

live.why: Output tokens drive latency as well as cost.

async.why: Output is billed at the higher rate.

stable.why: Compressing breaks the stable prefix that caching reuses.

unique.why: Long unique context is where compression pays.

live.why: The compression step adds compute and delay.

blocks.takeaway: Start with the lever that matches the shape of the spend. Caching for stable prefixes, routing for mixed difficulty, batch for delay-tolerant work, caps for output, compression for long unique inputs.

blocks.title: Say this out loud
blocks.md: Measure cost per successful task, not per token. A cheaper model can need more retries, longer outputs or more agent steps. Attribute tokens by consumer and by section of the prompt before you choose a lever, and say which lever the spend shape points to.

quiz.q: A chat re-sends the whole history each turn. Each turn adds 500 tokens, so turn k sends 500 x k input tokens. How many input tokens are sent across 20 turns?
quiz.explain: The sum 1 + 2 + ... + 20 is 210, so 500 x 210 = 105,000 input tokens. Only 10,000 of them are new content. The rest is re-reading, which is why an append-only prefix with caching, or compaction, changes the bill so much.

quiz.q: A nightly job scores 2 million documents against a long, shared instruction prompt. Nobody waits for the result, and a 24-hour turnaround is fine. Which approach lowers cost most?
options: Priority processing, because it gives the lowest latency for a very large evaluation run
A semantic cache across all documents, because they share one prefix
Batch with the shared instruction prefix first, accepting the 24-hour target
Provisioned throughput sized for the nightly peak and billed hourly, for stable speed
quiz.explain: Batch gives about 50% off for delay-tolerant work, and a stable prefix first can still earn cached-token pricing. Priority pays a premium for latency nobody needs. Documents differ, so a semantic cache would rarely match and could return the wrong document's answer. Provisioned capacity stays billed while idle, which is wasteful for a nightly job.

quiz.q: Tokens per task for an agent doubled after a release. Select every plausible driver.
options: Conversation history is re-sent on every model call
Tool results are appended to the context at each step
Hidden reasoning tokens count in the completion tokens
A shorter system prompt was shipped in the same release
quiz.explain: History, tool output and reasoning tokens all grow tokens per task, especially in loops. A shorter system prompt reduces tokens, so it cannot explain a doubling. Check calls per task and output tokens by step to see which one moved.

takeaways: Attribute tokens by sink and consumer before choosing a lever
Cost per successful task is the metric. Cost per token hides retries, loops and failures
History re-sent every turn grows with the square of the turn count, so keep the prefix append-only and cached
Routers split the prompt-cache prefix across models, so measure caching and routing together
Batch is the boring, large win for work nobody waits for
